descripcion_es: Saying that something exists (Spanish “hay”) with some and any.
resumen: There is and there are are the Spanish “hay”. Use there is with singular or uncountable nouns and there are with plurals. Negatives and questions usually have any; affirmatives have some.

explicacion.texto: In Spanish “hay” does not change, but in English the verb agrees with what comes after it: There is a bank (es: hay un banco), There are two banks (es: hay dos bancos). In the past: there was / there were.

filas: Yes, there is. / No, there isn't.
Yes, there are. / No, there aren't.

items: Some: affirmatives with plural and uncountable nouns (There's some bread).
Any: negatives and questions (Is there any coffee?).
With singular countable nouns use a/an: There's a cat.
In short affirmative answers, don't contract: Yes, there is.

ejemplos.frase: There's a supermarket at the end of the street.
ejemplos.traduccion: Hay un supermercado al final de la calle.

ejemplos.frase: There are thirty students in my class.
ejemplos.traduccion: Hay treinta alumnos en mi clase.

ejemplos.frase: Is there a chemist's near here?
There isn't any sugar in my coffee.
ejemplos.traduccion: No hay azúcar en mi café.

ejemplos.frase: There were a lot of people at the concert.
ejemplos.traduccion: Había mucha gente en el concierto.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: There is three books on the table.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: There are three books on the table.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With a plural, use there are.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: In my town have a castle.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: In my town there is a castle.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “hay” is not translated with have.

errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Is there a hotel near here?

ejercicios.frase: There ___ two bathrooms in the flat.
respuestas: are
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the main rule on the card: in English the verb agrees with what comes after it, unlike Spanish “hay”, which does not change. The clue is two bathrooms, a plural noun. That is why you use there are.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Two bathrooms is plural: there are.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hay dos cuartos de baño en el piso.

errores_previstos.respuesta: is
errores_previstos.explicacion: Two bathrooms is plural; there is only goes with singular and uncountable nouns.

errores_previstos.respuesta: have
errores_previstos.explicacion: Spanish “hay” is not translated with have; use there are.

errores_previstos.respuesta: be
errores_previstos.explicacion: You need the verb in the present plural: are.

ejercicios.frase: There ___ some water in the bottle.
respuestas: is
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the rule on the card: there is with singular or uncountable nouns. The clue is water, which is uncountable in English: it has no plural and no a. So, although in Spanish we might think of “aguas”, here you say there is some water. Some is there because the sentence is affirmative.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hay algo de agua en la botella.

errores_previstos.respuesta: are
errores_previstos.explicacion: Water is uncountable and takes a singular verb: there is.

errores_previstos.respuesta: has
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “hay”: in English you use there is, not has.

ejercicios.frase: There aren't ___ eggs in the fridge.
respuestas: any
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the rule in Rules and keys: any in negatives and questions, some in affirmatives. The clue is aren't, which makes the sentence negative. That is why you say there aren't any eggs. In Spanish you don't need any word (“no hay huevos”), but in English any is natural in this type of sentence.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hay huevos en la nevera.

errores_previstos.respuesta: some
errores_previstos.explicacion: Some is for affirmatives; negatives take any.

errores_previstos.respuesta: no
errores_previstos.explicacion: No is already negative; with aren't it would be a double negative. You would say there are no eggs or there aren't any eggs.

ejercicios.frase: There are ___ flowers on the table.
respuestas: some
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the rule of some in affirmatives with plural and uncountable nouns. The clue is there are, affirmative, followed by flowers, plural. Some here is the Spanish “unas” or “algunas”; in a negative or a question it would change to any.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In affirmatives with a plural, use some.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hay unas flores en la mesa.

errores_previstos.respuesta: any
errores_previstos.explicacion: Any is for negatives and questions; the sentence is affirmative, so use some.

errores_previstos.respuesta: a
errores_previstos.explicacion: A only goes with singular countable nouns; flowers is plural.

ejercicios.frase: There ___ a big storm last night.
respuestas: was
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the card's rule for the past: there was with singular and there were with plural. The clues are last night, which shows the past, and a big storm, singular. That is why you say there was.

errores_previstos.respuesta: were
errores_previstos.explicacion: Were is for plurals; a big storm is singular: there was.

errores_previstos.respuesta: is
errores_previstos.explicacion: Last night shows the past: there was.

errores_previstos.respuesta: had
errores_previstos.explicacion: Spanish “hubo” is not translated with had; use there was.

ejercicios.frase: ___ any good films on TV tonight?
respuestas: Are there
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the question row in the table: the order is inverted (Are there…?) and the verb agrees with the noun. The clues are the question mark, any (typical of questions) and films, which is plural. That is why it starts with Are there.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Question with a plural: Are there…?
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Hay alguna película buena en la tele esta noche?

por_opcion.Is there: Incorrect: it is for singular nouns; films is plural.
por_opcion.Are there: Correct: a question with a plural noun, verb before there.
por_opcion.There are: Incorrect: this is the order of a statement; in questions the verb goes first.

ejercicios.frase: There ___ a cat under the car.
respuestas: is
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the rule that singular countable nouns take a/an and there is. The clue is a cat, singular with an article. That is why the verb is is.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hay un gato debajo del coche.

por_opcion.are: Incorrect: are is for plurals; a cat is singular.
por_opcion.is: Correct: there is with a singular countable noun.
por_opcion.have: Incorrect: “there have a cat” is ungrammatical; Spanish “hay” is there is.

ejercicios.frase: Is there a bank near here? Yes, there ___.
respuestas: is
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the rule in Rules and keys: in short affirmative answers, don't contract. The clue is the short answer Yes, there… at the end of the sentence. That is why you say Yes, there is, never Yes, there's. In negatives you do contract: No, there isn't.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In short affirmative answers, don't contract.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Hay un banco cerca de aquí? Sí, lo hay.

por_opcion.is: Correct: the full form, required at the end of a short affirmative answer.
por_opcion.'s: Incorrect: the contraction can't go at the end of the sentence in an affirmative answer.
por_opcion.are: Incorrect: the question is about a bank, singular.

ejercicios.enunciado: Change the sentence into a question.
ejercicios.frase: There is a swimming pool in the hotel.
respuestas: Is there a swimming pool in the hotel?
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the question row in the table: the order is inverted and the verb goes before there (Is there…?). The rest of the sentence stays the same. You don't add do, because be makes questions by itself, and you can't leave out there.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Is a swimming pool in the hotel?
errores_previstos.explicacion: There is missing, and you can't leave it out (it is the typical mistake on the card).

errores_previstos.respuesta: There is a swimming pool in the hotel?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Only the intonation changes; in written English a question needs inversion: Is there.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Does there is a swimming pool in the hotel?
errores_previstos.explicacion: Be doesn't use do in questions: Is there.

ejercicios.enunciado: Change the sentence into a negative with any.
ejercicios.frase: There are some trees in the street.
respuestas: There aren't any trees in the street.
There are not any trees in the street.
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the rule of some and any: in a negative, some changes to any. To make the sentence negative, add not after are (aren't or are not). The result is there aren't any trees; both the contracted and the full form are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In a negative, some changes to any.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hay árboles en la calle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There aren't some trees in the street.
errores_previstos.explicacion: In negatives, some changes to any.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There isn't any trees in the street.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Trees is plural: aren't.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There don't are any trees in the street.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Be doesn't use do to make negatives: there aren't.

ejercicios.frase: There is many people in the square.
respuestas: There are many people in the square.
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the agreement rule on the card: there are with plurals. The clue is people, which is plural in English (the plural of person), although Spanish “gente” is singular. That is why you say there are many people.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hay mucha gente en la plaza.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There is many people in the square.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: people is plural and takes are.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There are many peoples in the square.
errores_previstos.explicacion: People is already plural; peoples means nations.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There is much people in the square.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Much and is treat people as uncountable, but it is a countable plural: many and are.

ejercicios.frase: There aren't some chairs in the room.
respuestas: There aren't any chairs in the room.
There are not any chairs in the room.
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the rule in Rules and keys: any in negatives, some in affirmatives. The sentence is already negative (aren't), so some must change to any. Both the contracted and the full form are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In negatives, use any, not some.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hay sillas en la habitación.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There aren't some chairs in the room.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: in negatives, use any.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There aren't no chairs in the room.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Double negative: with aren't, use any; or say there are no chairs.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There isn't any chairs in the room.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Chairs is plural: aren't.

ejercicios.frase: In the kitchen has a big window.
respuestas: In the kitchen there is a big window.
There is a big window in the kitchen.
There's a big window in the kitchen.
In the kitchen there's a big window.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the typical mistake on the card: Spanish “hay” is not translated with have or has. The original sentence copies Spanish, with the place at the start. You must use there is, which can go after the place phrase or at the start of the sentence; that is why several orders and the contraction there's are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Spanish “hay” is there is, not has.
ejercicios.traduccion: En la cocina hay una ventana grande.

errores_previstos.respuesta: In the kitchen has a big window.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: Spanish “hay” is there is, not has.

errores_previstos.respuesta: In the kitchen is a big window.
errores_previstos.explicacion: There is missing: it is the formal subject of the structure.

errores_previstos.respuesta: In the kitchen there are a big window.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A big window is singular: there is.

respuestas: There is a garden behind the house
Behind the house there is a garden
Is there a garden behind the house
ejercicios.explicacion: Use the basic order there is + noun + place. Because the words have no punctuation, three answers are accepted: the statement with the place at the end, the statement with the place at the start, and the question with inversion (Is there…). The important thing is that there and is go together and in the right order.
ejercicios.traduccion: Hay un jardín detrás de la casa. (También: Detrás de la casa hay un jardín; ¿Hay un jardín detrás de la casa?)

errores_previstos.respuesta: Behind the house is there a garden
errores_previstos.explicacion: In a statement there goes before is: behind the house there is a garden.

errores_previstos.respuesta: There is behind the house a garden
errores_previstos.explicacion: The noun goes right after there is and the place at the end.

descripcion_larga_es: There is and there are are the Spanish “hay”: they say that something exists or is in a place. Unlike Spanish, the verb agrees with what comes after it (singular or plural) and changes in the past (there was, there were). It is a basic structure for describing places, houses or towns. Spanish speakers find it hard because they tend to translate “hay” with have or to leave out there.

contexto.que_es: It is the structure that expresses existence or presence, like Spanish “hay”. It is formed with the formal subject there plus the verb be, which agrees with the noun that follows: there is with singular and uncountable nouns, there are with plurals. In the past: there was, there were.
contexto.por_que_importa: You need it from day one to describe your home, your neighbourhood or your town, ask about services (Is there a lift?) or say what is missing. Saying “In my town have a castle” or “Is a hotel near here?” is understood with effort but sounds very strange. It is always tested at beginner levels.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: Whenever you would say “hay” or “había” in Spanish: when describing places, saying what is in a room, asking if something exists or giving a short answer (Yes, there is). The signals are the idea of existence and a place phrase. Spanish speakers tend to use have, to leave the verb in the singular with plurals (“there is many people”) and to leave out there in questions.
